newsitem.title: SURINAM: Surinam steps into past with new president.
newsitem.headline: Surinam steps into past with new president.

text.p: Surinam turned back the clock on Thursday when national and regional politicians elected a leader of the former military government to run the country.

Jules Wijdenbosch, 55, who is backed by former military strongman Desi Bouterse, defeated current President Ronald Venetiaan by 438 votes to 407, in the closest presidential vote since independence from the Netherlands two decades ago.

The tense United People's Assembly ballot ended months of political uncertainty following unclear election results in May and handed Bouterse's National Democratic Party (NDP) its first ever victory at the polls.
Wijdenbosch, who will be sworn in Sept 14 for a five-year term, said he would consult all sections of society to reach a consensus government programme.
"We want as wide a government as possible," he told reporters after learning of the result.
Wijdenbosch won with the support of many former members of the ruling government coalition which began to unravel soon after scoring a small victory over the NDP in May's elections.
Wijdenbosch's running mate Pretaab Radakishun, who won the vice-presidential race in an uncontested vote, had been a leading member of Venetiaan's New Front coalition in national elections in May.
Those who defected to the NDP did so on condition that Bouterse hold no public office. He is held responsible by many for ordering the 1982 torture and murder of 15 opposition leaders.

His stern regime provoked an armed uprising by colourful rebel leader Ronny Brunswijk. The six-year conflict, which started in 1986, cost more than 500 lives and saw about 15,000 seek exile in neighbouring French Guiana.
Brunswijk took the result badly. "It's a major disappointment that Venetiaan lost. I still cannot believe it ... It's a political coup," he told Reuters.

Members of Brunswijk's now disbanded Jungle Commando rebel group have called for a return to arms in recent weeks if an NDP-led government does not stick to promises laid out in a 1992 peace agreement that ended the civil war.
Wijdenbosch's victory was expected to raise alarm in the Netherlands where the Dutch government has made its opposition to a Bouterse-sponsored government clear.
Bouterse, himself, congratulated the country on its new president and said that "now that the election is over, it is time to go to work because a lot has to be done."
A close friend of Bouterse, Wijdenbosch held several key cabinet posts in the puppet governments of the military regime.

Bouterse named Wijdenbosch vice-president and finance minister in the interim government installed after the so-called telephone coup on Christmas eve 1990 when military leaders rang government officials to tell them that the government had been overthrown.
During this period Wijdenbosch became famous for very lax fiscal policy as the government spent heavily on populist measures in an effort to garner support ahead of the 1991 elections.
By the time Venetiaan was installed, Wijdenbosch's policies had run down the central bank's reserves to zero and left the Surinamese guilder grossly overvalued.
Several opposition politicians said Wijdenbosch's government would cause a run on the local currency and see thousands of Surinamese try to leave the country.
But independent analysts said Bouterse and Wijdenbosch had probably learned from mistakes committed in the 1980s and would not wish to isolate the country again.
"It's very early to tell what will happen," said one Western diplomat who noted that Wijdenbosch will have the advantage of majority backing in the National Assembly.
